title: Sensors
subtitleHtml:
Introduction to Robotics (700.820), Lecture 2 — Narendiran Anandan, Serkan Ergun. Slides from winter term 2026 (26W, uploaded 13 Oct 2026).
Updated from the 25W version: new internal/external classification, a design question (eddy current vs capacitive), an automotive-radar demo, LIDAR and tactile-sensor slides; the variable-reluctance and FMCW-formula slides were dropped (kept at the end under Dropped from the 26W slides). Sections follow the 26W order.

headings.text: Displacement sensor – inductive: eddy current sensors
FMCW radar: further points and formulas

html:
The big picture

Every robot runs some version of SENSE → PLAN → ACT, and the three paradigms differ in how these are connected: hierarchical (sense, build a world model, plan, then act — slow but deliberate), reactive (sensing wired straight to action, no planning — fast but short-sighted) and hybrid (a planner on top sets goals, reactive behaviours below execute them). Sensing starts the chain. A sensor turns a physical quantity (the measurand) into a signal, usually electrical, and sensors are compared by how they're classified (internal/external, active/passive, contact/non-contact, absolute/relative), by their attributes (operating distance, invasiveness, output form) and by their performance (linearity, accuracy, repeatability, drift, hysteresis, responsiveness). The rest of the lecture is a catalogue of working principles: resistive, inductive and capacitive displacement sensors change a resistance, inductance or capacitance with position, and choosing between them depends on the environment (dust, liquids, clean room); time-of-flight sensors (ultrasound, laser) measure distance from an echo's travel time; optical encoders read angles digitally — with Gray code to avoid misreadings; radar, LIDAR and cameras give a picture of the surroundings; MEMS chips measure acceleration and rotation; GNSS (GPS and others) locates by trilateration; light sensors and tactile sensors close the list.

SENSE, PLAN, ACT

Robot primitiveInputOutput
SENSESensor dataSensed information
PLANInformation (sensed, cognitive)Directives
ACTDirectivesActuator commands
  • SENSE: takes the raw readings from the sensor and converts them into meaningful information about the world.
  • PLAN: based on sensed information and goals, generates directives.
  • ACT: based on directives, generates actuator commands.

Robot paradigms

  • A paradigm is a philosophy or set of assumptions and/or techniques which characterise an approach to a class of problems.

  • There are currently three paradigms for organising intelligence in robots:

    • Hierarchical
    • Reactive
    • Hybrid
  • They are generally described by the relationship between the three commonly accepted primitives of robotics: SENSE, PLAN, ACT.

Hierarchical paradigm

SENSE → PLAN → ACT, then back to SENSE: a strict loop.

  • Oldest paradigm.
  • Prevalent from 1967–1990.
  • This was based on an introspective view of how people think.
  • The robot senses the world, plans the next action and acts.
  • At each loop, the robot explicitly plans the next action.
  • All sensing data tends to be gathered into one global world model.
  • Constructing generic global models is a difficult problem.

Reactive paradigm

SENSE ↔ ACT, with no PLAN in between.

  • In this paradigm, the sensed information is directly coupled to output actions.
  • Started as an alternative approach to the hierarchical paradigm.
  • Heavily used in robotics research from 1988 to 1992.
  • Used by AI researchers to investigate biology and intelligence.
  • Helped by the rapidly decreasing cost of computer hardware and the increase in computing power.
  • Researchers could emulate frog and insect behaviour for about 500 dollars.

Hybrid paradigm

PLAN on top, connected to a SENSE ↔ ACT layer below.

  • Emerged in the 1990s.
  • Current area of research.
  • The robot first plans how best to decompose the task into a set of subtasks (mission planning), and then determines what the suitable behaviours are for accomplishing each subtask.
  • Then the behaviours start executing in parallel.
Why did the reactive paradigm appear, and why did hybrid win?

The hierarchical robot has to update its whole world model and re-plan before every action. That is slow, and in a changing world the plan is often outdated by the time it's executed: a robot that stops to think when a person steps in front of it is a robot that bumps into people. Reactive robots link a sensor reading directly to an action ("obstacle close → turn away"), so they respond instantly. But with no plan they can't pursue long-term goals and may get stuck going in circles. Hybrid systems combine both: slow, deliberate planning decides what to do (the route), and fast reactive behaviours handle how, moment to moment (avoiding obstacles on the way).

Worked example: which paradigm is this?
  • A robot vacuum that turns whenever its bumper is pressed, with no map: sensing directly triggers action, nothing is planned → reactive.
  • A factory arm that waits for a camera image, computes a full path, then executes it, and only then looks again: strict sense–plan–act loop → hierarchical.
  • A delivery robot that plans its route through the building, then follows it while dodging people with its distance sensors: planning on top, reactive behaviours below → hybrid.

Deciding question: is there a PLAN step, and does it sit between sensing and every action (hierarchical), above running behaviours (hybrid), or nowhere (reactive)?

Sensors and actuators

  • Sensors are devices that produce an output signal in response to some physical parameter in the environment: light, temperature, distance, velocity, acceleration, angle, sound, more…
  • An actuator is a device that produces a motion by converting energy and signals going into the system.

Sensor

Environmental variable (measurand) → interface with environment → sensing element → signal conditioner (optional) → output interface (usually electrical) → output signal

Example system: a thermocouple (50 µV/°C) feeds an amplifier; a processor with signal conditioning, A/D converter, program logic and a PWM output drives a fan motor via an output driver.

The slides also show a camera module and an image sensor chip as a sensor example.

Intuition: why the chain has so many boxes

The sensing element alone rarely gives a usable signal. A thermocouple, for instance, delivers about 50\,\mu\mathrm{V} per °C — far too small for a processor to read directly. Signal conditioning amplifies and filters it, the A/D converter turns it into a number, and only then can the program decide what to do (here: drive a fan with PWM). Many of the problems in 9 Measurement and Signal Processing happen in these middle boxes.

Sensor classification

They can be classified in a number of ways:

  • Internal or external
  • Active or passive
  • Contact or noncontact
  • Absolute or relative
  • Function
  • Physical phenomena
Intuition: the four yes/no classifications
  • Internal vs external: an internal (proprioceptive) sensor measures the robot's own state: joint angles, wheel rotations, motor current, battery voltage. An external (exteroceptive) sensor measures the environment: distances to obstacles, camera images, contact with an object. Same physics can serve both: a potentiometer in a joint is internal, a potentiometer in a whisker that bends when it hits a wall is external.
  • Active vs passive: an active sensor sends out its own energy and measures what comes back (ultrasound, laser, radar); a passive one only receives what's already there (camera, thermometer, photodiode).
  • Contact vs non-contact: does it have to touch what it measures (potentiometer, bumper) or not (capacitive, laser)?
  • Absolute vs relative: an absolute sensor reports the actual value right after switching on (absolute encoder, GPS); a relative one only reports changes from wherever it started (incremental encoder), so it needs a reference first.

Sensor attributes

Measurand

  • Positional and dimensional — linear displacement, angular displacement, liquid level, area, volume
  • Proximity — metal detection
  • Static mechanical — mass, pressure, torque
  • Dynamic mechanical — velocity, acceleration, flow rate
  • Thermal — temperature, temperature variation
  • Electromagnetic — wavelength, frequency, intensity, polarisation (particularly optical and infrared)
  • Electrostatic — charge, capacitance, resistance
  • Magnetic — flux
  • Sonic/acoustic — sound frequency, intensity and direction

Operating distance

  • Remote sensing — few meters to millions of kilometres.

    • Only option when the measurand is always distant (astronomical and navigational).
    • Background noise is present when large distances are involved.
  • Near-contact sensing — few millimetres to few meters.
  • Contact sensing — touching the measurand.

Invasiveness

  • Sensor invasiveness: the degree to which the sensor reacts with the measurand environment in which it is placed.
  • Measurand invasiveness: the measurand can damage the sensor in a hostile environment (radiation, acidity, high temperature, chemicals).
Intuition: invasiveness works both ways

Sensor invasiveness: the sensor changes what it measures — a cold thermometer dipped into a few drops of hot water cools them down, so it reads too low. Measurand invasiveness: the measured environment harms the sensor — acid eating a probe, radiation damaging electronics.

Form of output signal

  • Mechanical

  • Electrical:

    • Analog: voltage or current dependent; modulated by frequency or amplitude
    • Digital: binary coded; Gray coded

The slide lists the numbers 0–15 in decimal, binary and Gray code (table below, in the encoder section).

Sensor performance characteristics

  • Linearity/nonlinearity

Three example input–output curves: a straight line y = 1.2x, a curve y = 0.1x^2 + 0.03x, and scattered measurements following y = 1.5x^2 - 40.7x + 11006.

  • Range of operational accuracy
  • Drift, hysteresis
  • Responsiveness
  • Reliability
  • Repeatability and reproducibility

The second slide also shows a slowly curving input–output plot.

Intuition: what each characteristic means
  • Linearity: output proportional to input (y = kx). Convenient, because one factor converts output back to input everywhere. A non-linear sensor needs a calibration curve.
  • Range: the span of inputs over which the stated accuracy holds.
  • Repeatability: the same input, measured repeatedly under the same conditions, gives the same output. Reproducibility: the same, but under changed conditions (another day, operator, device).
  • Drift: the output slowly changes over time although the input doesn't.
  • Hysteresis: the output depends on whether you approach a value from below or from above.
  • Responsiveness: how quickly the output follows a change of the input.
Common mistake: accuracy vs repeatability

A sensor can be very repeatable yet inaccurate: it always reads 2\,\mathrm{cm} too long, but always exactly the same. That's a systematic error, and calibration removes it. A sensor whose readings scatter randomly can't be fixed by calibration; you can only average many readings. Repeatability is about the spread, accuracy about the distance to the true value.

Sensor ergonomic and economic factors

  • Human–machine interfaces
  • Ease of installation and repairing
  • Cost
  • Packaging
  • Market volume

Displacement sensing – resistive

R = \rho \frac{l}{A}
Symbols
  • R — electrical resistance (Ω); in a potentiometer, the resistance between one end and the sliding contact (wiper)
  • \rho — resistivity of the resistive material (Ω·m)
  • l — length of resistive track the current flows through (m) — this is what changes with the displacement, so R tracks position linearly
  • A — cross-sectional area of the track (m²)

Potentiometers: (a) a linear one, with a wiper sliding along a resistive element; (b) a rotary one, with a dead zone where the element is interrupted.

Advantages:

  • Easy to use
  • Low cost
  • Simple circuit
  • High-amplitude output signal
  • Proven technology

Disadvantages:

  • Limited bandwidth
  • Frictional loading
  • Inertial loading
  • Wear and tear

*The slide asks: Internal or external?*

How does a potentiometer turn position into a voltage?

A voltage V_{in} is applied across the whole resistive element; the wiper picks off the voltage at its position. Since R = \rho\,l/A, the resistance up to the wiper is proportional to the length l it covers, so the output is a fraction of V_{in} proportional to position: V_{out} = V_{in} \cdot \frac{x}{L} (a voltage divider). Example: 10\,\mathrm{V} across a 100\,\mathrm{mm} track, wiper at 30\,\mathrm{mm} → 3\,\mathrm{V}. The wiper rubs on the track, which explains the disadvantages: friction, wear, and a limited speed (bandwidth).

Is a potentiometer an internal or an external sensor?

It depends on what it is attached to, not on how it works. Mounted on a robot's joint or motor shaft, it reports the robot's own joint angle → internal, its most common use in robots (servo motors contain one). Used as a probe that is pushed in by an object, or in a joystick a person moves, it measures something outside the robot → external. The classification is about what is measured, not the working principle.

Linear Variable Differential Transformer (LVDT)

A primary winding between two secondary windings, with a movable core inside.

  • \pm 0.25\,\mathrm{mm} to \pm 7.5\,\mathrm{cm} range.
  • -265\,^\circ\mathrm{C} to 600\,^\circ\mathrm{C} operating temperature.
  • Radiation-resistant designs are available.

The slide also shows the output voltage against position — a straight line through zero — and the circuit: an AC source, absolute-value stages and filters for each secondary, and a difference amplifier.

Intuition: how an LVDT measures position

The primary coil is driven with AC and induces voltages in both secondaries through the iron core. With the core centred, both secondaries get the same voltage, and their difference is zero. Push the core to one side and that secondary couples more strongly: the difference grows in proportion to the displacement, and its sign (phase) tells you the direction. There's no sliding contact, so — unlike a potentiometer — there's no wear.

Displacement sensor – inductive: eddy current sensors

  • Excitation in the sensor coil induces eddy currents in the target surface.
  • The eddy currents generate an opposing magnetic field that affects the coil inductance.
  • The change in inductance can be measured to obtain the target distance.
  • Range: 0.4 to 80 mm
  • Resolution: 0.5 µm
  • High linearity and temperature stability.
  • High-speed applications.
  • Since the target material, shape, etc. influence the output, it is necessary to calibrate the system statistically for a specific target.
Intuition: why the target must be metal

The sensor coil's alternating field induces eddy currents only in an electrically conductive target. These currents create their own field against the coil's, and the closer the target, the stronger the effect. Anything non-conductive in the gap (air, dust, water, oil, plastic) is practically invisible to the sensor. That is both its strength (it doesn't care about dirt) and its limit (it can't see non-metal targets, and different metals need their own calibration).

Proximity and displacement sensing – capacitive

  • Capacitance is the ability of a component or circuit to collect and store energy in the form of an electrical charge:
C = \varepsilon \frac{A}{d}

(Two plates of area A at distance d, with permittivity \varepsilon between them.)

Symbols
  • C — capacitance (F, farad = C/V): charge stored per volt
  • \varepsilon — permittivity of the material between the plates (F/m); for air \approx \varepsilon_0 = 8.85 \cdot 10^{-12} F/m
  • A — overlapping area of the plates (m²); d — distance between them (m)

The slide also shows how capacitive touch sensing works: a finger near transmit and receive electrodes changes the mutual capacitance between them (or the self-capacitance of a single electrode).

Capacitive displacement sensors — the capacitance changes when…

  • the gap changes: C = \varepsilon \frac{A}{x}
  • the overlap changes (one plate slides sideways by x): C = \varepsilon \frac{A - wx}{d}, where w is the plate width
  • the dielectric between the plates moves in or out.

Commercial capacitive displacement sensors (from Micro-Epsilon):

  • Non-contact
  • High accuracy (the slide quotes 0.04 nm resolution)
  • Vacuum and clean-room applications
  • Immune to magnetic field interference
Gap or overlap: which one gives a linear sensor?

Look at where the displacement appears in the formula. With overlap, C = \varepsilon\frac{A - wx}{d} is a straight line in x: equal steps give equal changes in C. With the gap, C = \varepsilon\frac{A}{x} is a hyperbola: halving the gap doubles C, so the sensor is very sensitive at small gaps and much less at large ones — non-linear, but excellent for tiny movements.

Question: eddy current or capacitive?

You are designing a robot to be used in an industrial manufacturing process. You need to measure the distance to copper plates with sub-millimetre precision within a range of 0–10 mm. Which sensor would you choose, an eddy current sensor or a capacitive sensor?

  • (a) The plate has just arrived from a washing process to clean off all dust.
  • (b) The plate is in a climate-controlled clean room.
Worked example — choosing between the two (the slide gives no answer; this is my reading)
  1. Check what both sensors need. Copper is a good conductor, so both work in principle: eddy current sensors need a conductive target, capacitive sensors measure the gap to a conductive plate. Both cover 0–10 mm with sub-millimetre resolution (eddy current: range 0.4–80 mm, resolution 0.5 µm).
  2. Ask what else is in the gap. A capacitive sensor measures C = \varepsilon \frac{A}{d}, so it reacts to anything that changes \varepsilon between sensor and plate. An eddy current sensor only reacts to the conductive target.
  3. (a) Just washed: the plate may still carry a film of water (\varepsilon_r \approx 80 against \approx 1 for air) or cleaning residue. For a 1 mm gap, a 10 µm water film already makes a capacitive sensor read about 10 µm too close, and drops or streaks make it worse and unpredictable. The eddy current sensor ignores the water → eddy current sensor.
  4. (b) Clean room: the gap holds only clean, dry, climate-controlled air, so \varepsilon is constant. Now the capacitive sensor's advantages count: higher resolution (down to nm), any conductive target without per-material calibration, and it is built for vacuum and clean-room use (slide 23) → capacitive sensor.

Deciding question: can something other than air get between sensor and target? If yes, eddy current; if the gap is guaranteed clean and dry, capacitive for the best precision.

Ultrasound displacement transducer

An oscillator and amplifier drive the transmitter (Tr); the echo from the object returns to the receiver (Re); electronics measure the elapsed time and calculate d.

Transducer types:

  • Mechanical — whistles, sirens
  • Electromagnetic — microphone
  • Piezoelectric — quartz, ceramics, etc.
  • Electrostatic — capacitor with free membrane

Time-of-flight techniques: pulse echo, phase angle, frequency modulation.

Pictured: a hobby ultrasound module with separate transmitter and receiver, and round ultrasonic transducers.

How does the time-of-flight principle give a distance?

The sensor sends a pulse and measures the time t until the echo returns. The sound travels to the object and back, a distance 2d, so 2d = v\,t, i.e. d = \frac{v\,t}{2}. In air, sound travels at about 343\,\mathrm{m/s}. The same principle works with light (laser range finder, lidar), where v = c — only the times are much shorter.

Worked example: time of flight with sound and with light
  • Ultrasound: an echo returns after t = 5.8\,\mathrm{ms}. Distance d = \frac{343 \cdot 0.0058}{2}\,\mathrm{m} \approx 1.0\,\mathrm{m}.
  • Laser: an object 3\,\mathrm{m} away returns the light after t = \frac{2d}{c} = \frac{6}{3 \cdot 10^8}\,\mathrm{s} = 20\,\mathrm{ns}.

What it shows: to resolve centimetres, an ultrasound sensor must time to about a tenth of a millisecond; a laser sensor needs well under a nanosecond. That's why laser range finders need fast, expensive electronics.

Common mistake: forgetting the factor 2

d = v \cdot t gives twice the distance: t is the round-trip time. Also: the speed of sound depends on air temperature (it rises about 0.6\,\mathrm{m/s} per °C), so precise ultrasound sensors compensate for temperature.

Laser range finder

  • Measurement method: time of flight.
  • Range: a few meters to a few kilometers.
  • Resolution: 10 mm.
  • Line-of-sight measurement.
  • Expensive.

  • Applications:

    • Production and control
    • 3D mapping
    • High-precision guidance
d = \frac{c\,t}{2}
Symbols
  • d — distance to the target (m)
  • c — speed of light (\approx 3 \cdot 10^8\,\mathrm{m/s})
  • t — measured round-trip time of the laser pulse (s); divided by 2 because the light travels to the target and back

Optical encoder displacement sensors

  • Optical encoders are used to measure either angular or linear positions.
  • Those used for angular detection are commonly called rotary or shaft encoders.
  • They use light as the means to transform movement into electrical signals.
  • All devices have two basic building blocks: a main grating and a detection system. It is the position of one with respect to the other that is detected.
  • Types: incremental or absolute.
Intuition: incremental vs absolute encoders

An incremental encoder has one pattern of evenly spaced slits and just produces a pulse per step; the controller counts the pulses. It only knows how far it has moved since it started counting (relative), and loses its position if power fails. An absolute encoder has several tracks that together spell out a code for each position, so it knows the exact angle immediately (absolute).

Absolute encoders: direct binary encoder

(a) Four tracks with weights 2^0 to 2^3 encode positions 0–15; (b) the triangular photodetector output of the 2^0 track; (c) the same signal converted into a square wave.

  • Has N tracks, each providing one bit of a direct binary number.
  • For each track, the readout unit consists of a light source, a mask and a photodetector.
  • As the mask moves over a clear region on the grating, the photodetector output increases and decreases.
  • The truncated triangular wave output is converted to a square wave output using a suitable threshold.

The problem at a transition: between 7 (0111) and 8 (1000) all four bits change. If the readout heads are not perfectly aligned, the encoder may briefly read 1001 = 9 or 1101 = 13 instead of a clean 7 → 8.

Absolute encoders: Gray code

DecimalBinaryGrayDecimalBinaryGray
000000000810001100
100010001910011101
2001000111010101111
3001100101110111110
4010001101211001010
5010101111311011011
6011001011411101001
7011101001511111000

The slides also show the V-scan encoder (two staggered readout heads per track, with logic picking the right one) and a Gray code encoder disc.

Why does Gray code solve the transition problem?

In Gray code, neighbouring numbers differ in exactly one bit: 7 = 0100 and 8 = 1100. At any transition only one track changes, so a slightly misaligned head can only produce either the old or the new value — never a number far away, like 13. Even the wrap-around from 15 (1000) back to 0 (0000) changes just one bit.

Worked example: binary to Gray code

Rule: keep the first (leftmost) bit; each following Gray bit is 1 if the binary bit and the one to its left differ, else 0 (XOR of neighbours).

  • 6 = 0110: first bit 0; then 0 vs 1 → 1, 1 vs 1 → 0, 1 vs 0 → 1 → Gray 0101 ✓ (table).
  • 11 = 1011: 1; 1 vs 0 → 1; 0 vs 1 → 1; 1 vs 1 → 0 → Gray 1110 ✓.

In code: gray = b ^ (b >> 1).

FMCW radar

  • Can measure very small ranges to the target.
  • Can measure simultaneously the target range and its relative velocity.
  • Very high accuracy of range measurement.

A chirp: the frequency rises linearly from f_c = 77\,\mathrm{GHz} to 81\,\mathrm{GHz} (bandwidth B = 4\,\mathrm{GHz}) during T_c = 40\,\mu\mathrm{s}; the slope is S. The slide also shows a radar module and its circuit board.

Intuition: ranging with a frequency instead of a stopwatch

FMCW = frequency-modulated continuous wave. Instead of timing a short pulse, the radar sends a continuous chirp whose frequency rises steadily. The echo is the same chirp, delayed by the round trip \tau = 2d/c. At any instant, the transmitted signal is therefore a little higher in frequency than the received one, and that difference is proportional to the delay, i.e. to the distance. Measuring a frequency difference of a few MHz is much easier than timing a few nanoseconds. A moving target additionally shifts the echo's frequency and phase (Doppler effect), which is how range and relative velocity come out together. (The formulas are under Dropped from the 26W slides.)

Automotive radar demo (ViSight)

Slide 32: a still from an automotive radar demo. Left, the camera view of a motorway; right, the radar view: a top-down map of detected points (lateral position −30 to 30 m, colour = height), with moving objects shown in yellow.

Connection

This is what makes radar the standard sensor for adaptive cruise control: it sees cars ahead at long range, measures their speed directly, and works in rain, fog and darkness where cameras struggle. Its picture is coarse, though, which is why cars combine it with cameras (and sometimes LIDAR).

LIDAR

A self-driving car surrounded by a LIDAR point cloud: rings of points on the road, buildings and trees, coloured by height.

Intuition: a laser range finder that sweeps

LIDAR (light detection and ranging) is the laser range finder from above, scanned in many directions: rotating or steered laser beams measure time of flight d = \frac{c\,t}{2} hundreds of thousands of times per second. Each measurement is one point at a known angle and distance, so together they form a 3D point cloud of the surroundings. The rings on the road in the picture come from beams at fixed elevation angles sweeping around the car.

Vision

  • Vision sensors provide the richest information.
  • Single camera / stereo camera
  • Geometric information
  • Texture
  • Colour

  • Applications:

    • Distance measurement
    • Object detection, recognition
    • Control
Connection

Turning a camera's pixels into "object here, 2 m away" is a job for the methods in 10 Introduction to AI and the signal processing of 9 Measurement and Signal Processing. Raw camera data is rich but needs the most processing of all the sensors in this lecture.

MEMS accelerometers and gyroscope

  • MEMS: Micro-ElectroMechanical System.

The slides show a tiny chip on a fingertip, a model of a MEMS accelerometer (a suspended mass with fixed comb plates), and an electron-microscope image of the comb structure.

MEMS accelerometer

Accelerometer gradeMain applicationBandwidthg-range
ConsumerMotion, static acceleration0 Hz1 g
AutomotiveCrash/stability100 Hz<200 g / 2 g
IndustrialPlatform stability/tilt5 Hz to 500 Hz25 g
TacticalWeapons/craft navigation<1 kHz8 g
NavigationSubmarine/craft navigation>300 Hz15 g
Intuition: a capacitive sensor in disguise

A MEMS accelerometer is a tiny proof mass on springs, with comb-shaped fingers interleaved with fixed fingers. When the chip accelerates, the mass lags behind (inertia, F = ma), the springs bend, and the gaps between the fingers change. That changes the capacitance (C = \varepsilon A/d from above), which the chip measures. Gravity pulls the mass too, so at rest an accelerometer reads 1\,g downwards — that's how a phone knows which way is up.

Global navigation

Global Positioning System (GPS)

  • GPS is a system of 30+ navigation satellites circling Earth.
  • We know where they are because they constantly send out signals.
  • A GPS receiver listens for these signals.
  • Once the receiver calculates its distance from four or more GPS satellites, it can figure out where you are using trilateration.

Three satellites, each with a circle of known distance around it; the receiver sits where the circles intersect.

GLONASS, Galileo, BeiDou

(On the 26W slides this comes after the MEMS slides; kept next to GPS here.)

  • GPS emerged from the US military, and was made publicly available.
  • Accuracy for consumers: a few meters; for the military: (sub-)millimeter.
  • GLONASS: Russia
  • Galileo: EU
  • BeiDou: China
  • IRNSS: India (in planning), QZSS: Japan (in planning)
  • Most devices use a combination of the navigation systems.
  • Local restrictions (devices in Russia must have GLONASS enabled, devices in China need BeiDou).
Why does a GPS receiver need four satellites, not three?

Each satellite's signal says when it was sent; the receiver measures when it arrived, and the travel time × the speed of light gives the distance. Three distances would fix a point in 3D. But the receiver's own clock is cheap and not exactly in sync with the satellites' atomic clocks, and an error of a millionth of a second already means 300\,\mathrm{m}. So there are four unknowns — x, y, z and the receiver's clock error — and four measurements are needed to solve for them.

Unclear (slide 38)

The slide claims "(sub-)millimeter" accuracy for the military. Military receivers are more accurate than consumer ones, but real-time positioning from satellite signals alone is at the level of decimetres to metres. Millimetre-level results come from special surveying techniques (carrier-phase measurements, reference stations, long averaging), not from military access as such.

Light sensors (reverse LED)

  • Photoresistors — their resistance drops strongly as light intensity rises (graph on the slide, from darkness to bright sunlight).
  • Photodiodes — with reverse voltage, the diode current grows with the light (lumens); with no light only a small dark current flows.
  • Phototransistor

Tactile sensors

A robotic hand, a two-finger gripper and a parallel gripper with pads of tactile sensors on the fingertips, plus loose sensor modules.

The slide also shows a GelSight Mini (an optical tactile sensor), dome-shaped sensor designs with an LED and a light-dependent resistor (LDR) under a soft cover, a fingertip sensor, and a layered sensor of conductive stripes on a flexible substrate.

Intuition: how a robot feels contact

A tactile sensor measures contact, pressure and its distribution over a surface, like the skin of a fingertip. The principles are the ones from this lecture, arranged in grids: resistive (a pressure-sensitive layer whose resistance drops when squeezed, read at the crossing points of conductive stripes), capacitive (pressing reduces the gap d between two electrodes, so C rises) and optical (a soft dome or gel deforms; an LED and photodetector, or in GelSight a small camera, see the change in light). Grippers need them to hold an egg without crushing it and to notice when something is slipping.

Dropped from the 26W slides

These slides were in the 25W deck but are no longer in 26W. Kept for reference.

Displacement sensors – inductive: variable reluctance

Single-coil variable reluctance displacement sensor

  • A basic inductive sensor consists of a magnetic circuit made from a ferromagnetic core with a coil wound on it.
  • The coil generates and drives flux through the magnetic circuit, through the core and the air gap.
  • The presence of the air gap causes a large increase in circuit reluctance and a corresponding decrease in the flux.
  • Hence, small variations in the air gap result in measurable changes in inductance:
L = \frac{L_0}{1 + \alpha d}

(d: air gap; L_0 and \alpha are constants of the sensor.)

Symbols
  • L — inductance of the coil (H, henry)
  • L_0 — the inductance with zero air gap (H), a constant of the sensor
  • \alpha — a sensor constant (1/m) setting how strongly the gap matters
  • d — width of the air gap (m), the quantity being measured

Differential variable reluctance displacement sensor

L_1 = \frac{L_{10}}{1 + \alpha(d + x)}, \qquad L_2 = \frac{L_{20}}{1 + \alpha(d - x)}
Symbols
  • L_1, L_2 — inductances of the two coils (H)
  • L_{10}, L_{20} — their zero-gap inductances (H, sensor constants)
  • d — the air gap of each coil when the armature is centred (m)
  • x — displacement of the armature from the centre (m): it widens one gap (d + x) and narrows the other (d - x)
  • \alpha — sensor constant, as above
  • A linear output can be obtained from L_1 and L_2 for small displacements using appropriate circuits.
  • Continuous resolution
  • High output
  • Affected by external magnetic fields
  • A typical sensor of this type has an input span of 1 cm, a coil inductance of 25 mH, and a coil resistance of 75 Ω.
Why use two coils instead of one?

One coil gives L = \frac{L_0}{1 + \alpha d}, which is not linear in the gap. With two coils, moving the core by x widens one gap and narrows the other: one inductance falls while the other rises. Comparing the two (taking their difference) cancels most of the curvature, so the result is close to proportional to x for small movements. Effects that hit both coils equally — like temperature — also largely cancel. The same idea is behind the LVDT.

FMCW radar: further points and formulas

  • (the minimal measured range is comparable to the transmitted wavelength)
  • Signal processing after mixing is performed at a low frequency range, considerably simplifying the realization of the processing circuits.
  • Safety from the absence of pulse radiation with a high peak power.

How it works: (1) a synthesizer generates the chirp, (2) the TX antenna sends it, (3) the RX antenna receives the echo, delayed by \tau, (4) a mixer combines the transmitted and received signal into the IF signal.

x_1 = \sin(\omega_1 t + \theta_1), \qquad x_2 = \sin(\omega_2 t + \theta_2)
x_{out} = \sin\big[(\omega_1 - \omega_2)t + (\theta_1 - \theta_2)\big]
Symbols
  • x_1, x_2 — the two signals entering the mixer: transmitted chirp and received echo (normalised amplitude)
  • \omega_1, \omega_2 — their angular frequencies at that instant (rad/s); \theta_1, \theta_2 — their phases (rad)
  • t — time (s)
  • x_{out} — the mixer output (the IF signal): its frequency is the difference of the two input frequencies, its phase the difference of the phases
\tau = \frac{2d}{c}, \qquad f_0 = \frac{2Sd}{c}, \qquad \theta_0 = \frac{4\pi d}{\lambda}
Symbols
  • \tau — round-trip delay of the echo (s)
  • d — distance to the object (m); c — speed of light (\approx 3 \cdot 10^8\,\mathrm{m/s}); 2d because the signal travels there and back
  • S — chirp slope: how fast the frequency rises (Hz/s), S = B / T_c
  • f_0 — frequency of the IF signal (Hz), proportional to d
  • \theta_0 — phase of the IF signal (rad); \lambda — wavelength of the radar signal (m, about 4 mm at 77 GHz)

The IF signal is A\sin(2\pi f_0 t + \theta_0): a constant frequency f_0 proportional to the distance.

Why is the IF frequency proportional to the distance?

The echo is an exact copy of the chirp, delayed by \tau = \frac{2d}{c}. Since both chirps rise with the same slope S, at every moment the transmitted frequency is ahead of the received one by the same amount S\tau. The mixer outputs exactly that difference: f_0 = S\tau = \frac{2Sd}{c}. Measuring a frequency of a few MHz is far easier than timing a delay of a few nanoseconds directly — which is the advantage listed on the slide.

Worked example: from IF frequency to distance

Slide chirp: S = \frac{B}{T_c} = \frac{4 \cdot 10^9\,\mathrm{Hz}}{40 \cdot 10^{-6}\,\mathrm{s}} = 10^{14}\,\mathrm{Hz/s}.

  • Target at d = 3\,\mathrm{m}: f_0 = \frac{2 \cdot 10^{14} \cdot 3}{3 \cdot 10^8}\,\mathrm{Hz} = 2\,\mathrm{MHz}.
  • Backwards: an IF frequency of 1\,\mathrm{MHz} means d = \frac{f_0\,c}{2S} = 1.5\,\mathrm{m}.

Twice the distance, twice the frequency: the range is read off a frequency.
